hook: Fly over the western United States and Canada and you will not see their border, yet for about 2,000 kilometers it runs along one line of latitude, 49° N. In Germany, a strip of old watchtowers marks a border that has not existed since 1990. Every boundary has a history: when it was drawn, who drew it and what it follows. Geographers sort boundaries into types by that history.

options: A country with people, territory, a government and recognition
prereq.why: States are the basic units of the political map.

options: The visible marks people leave on the land
prereq.why: Buildings, roads, fields and walls are all part of the cultural landscape.

figure.caption: Six boundary types, sorted by when a boundary was drawn, who drew it and what it follows.

chain.cause: A boundary is drawn before many settlers arrive
chain.effect: it is antecedent, and settlement later grows up around it

chain.cause: Outside powers draw a boundary without asking the people who live there
chain.effect: it is superimposed and may cut a people in two

chain.cause: A boundary stops working but its walls or fences remain
chain.effect: it becomes a relict boundary, visible in the cultural landscape

ideas: Sort by timing: antecedent boundaries come before settlement; subsequent ones come after.
Sort by what it follows: consequent boundaries follow a cultural line (India and Pakistan, 1947); geometric ones are straight lines (49° N).
Sort by who drew it: superimposed boundaries are forced by outside powers (much of Africa). A relict boundary no longer works (the old East and West German line).
One boundary can fit more than one type: Kenya and Tanzania is geometric and superimposed.

misconception.wrong: Every boundary fits exactly one type.
misconception.right: The types describe different things (timing, what it follows, who drew it), so one boundary can fit two or three. The US and Canada line along 49° N is both geometric and antecedent.

summary: Political boundaries mark where one state's territory ends. Geographers sort them by history: antecedent boundaries come before settlement and subsequent ones after; consequent boundaries follow cultural lines and geometric ones follow straight lines; superimposed boundaries are forced by outside powers, and relict boundaries no longer work but still show on the land. Many boundaries fit more than one type.
